lessonTitle: Isentropic Flow and Nozzles: Stagnation Conditions, Choking and Area Change

blocks.text: The nozzle of a small cold-gas thruster fed from a 500 kPa tank passes exactly the same mass flow whether the thruster is fired into a vacuum or into a pressurised chamber at 250 kPa. Past a certain pressure ratio the flow simply stops responding to what happens downstream. This unit explains that choking and the compressible-flow relations behind it.

blocks.markdown: When gas moves at speeds comparable to the speed of sound, its density changes with pressure and the flow must be treated as **compressible**. We consider steady, one-dimensional flow of a perfect gas with constant specific heat ratio $\gamma$ (1.4 for air) and gas constant $R$ (287 J/(kg K) for air), and we assume the flow is **isentropic**: adiabatic and frictionless, and therefore reversible. The key dimensionless number is the **Mach number** $M=V/a$, where $V$ is flow speed (m/s) and $a=\sqrt{\gamma RT}$ is the local speed of sound, with $T$ in kelvin.

blocks.title: Stagnation (total) conditions
blocks.text: The stagnation temperature $T_0$ and stagnation pressure $p_0$ are the values the gas would reach if it were brought to rest adiabatically (and, for $p_0$, isentropically). From the energy equation $c_pT+V^2/2=c_pT_0$ with $c_p=\gamma R/(\gamma-1)$, the static temperature $T$ (the temperature a thermometer moving with the gas reads) is related to $T_0$ as shown below.

blocks.caption: Isentropic stagnation relations (T in K, p absolute)

blocks.title: Stagnation conditions on an aircraft
blocks.prompt: An aircraft flies at Mach 0.80 where the static temperature is 230 K and the static pressure is 30.0 kPa. Treat the air as a perfect gas (gamma 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg K)). Find the flight speed and the stagnation temperature and pressure.

steps.text: Speed of sound at the static temperature, then the flight speed.
Stagnation pressure ratio is the same bracket raised to the power 3.5 (gamma/(gamma-1)).

blocks.markdown: **Choking.** In a converging nozzle fed from a large reservoir at $p_0,T_0$, lowering the back pressure increases the flow until the throat reaches $M=1$ (sonic), the **critical** condition. For air this occurs when the back pressure falls to $p^*/p_0=(2/(\gamma+1))^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}=0.528$. At that point the flow rate is the maximum the throat of area $A^*$ can pass, and any further reduction in back pressure cannot be communicated upstream because the information (a pressure wave) travels at the speed of sound, which is only equal to the flow speed at the throat.

blocks.caption: Choked mass flow rate; also T*/T0 = 2/(gamma+1) = 0.833 and p*/p0 = 0.528 for air

blocks.title: Choked flow through a throat
blocks.prompt: A tank holds air at p0 = 500 kPa (absolute) and T0 = 300 K and discharges through a converging nozzle with a throat diameter of 20 mm into a low-pressure region. Show that the flow is choked and find the mass flow rate and throat temperature.

steps.text: Compare the critical pressure with the available back pressure: p* = 0.528 x 500 = 264 kPa. Any back pressure below this (for example a near-vacuum) gives choked flow.
Choked mass flow using the air form of the formula.
Throat static temperature at M = 1 is T0 times 2/(gamma+1); the sonic speed there equals the throat velocity.

blocks.answer: Choked; mass flow = 0.367 kg/s, T* = 250.0 K, V* = 317 m/s.

blocks.markdown: **Effect of area change.** Combining the continuity equation $\rho VA=\text{const}$ with the momentum equation $dp=-\rho V\,dV$ and the speed of sound relation $dp=a^2d\rho$ gives the area-velocity relation $\dfrac{dA}{A}=(M^2-1)\dfrac{dV}{V}$. At $M<1$ density changes are small compared with velocity changes, so the flow behaves as an incompressible one: a converging duct speeds the flow up. At $M>1$ density falls faster than velocity rises, so more area is needed to pass the mass flow while speeding the flow up.

rows: Can only occur at a minimum area (throat)
Reached at the throat of a converging-diverging nozzle
blocks.caption: Response of one-dimensional isentropic flow to area change

items: Find $a=\sqrt{\gamma RT}$ and $M=V/a$ from the static temperature.
Use $T_0/T$ and $p_0/p$ to move between static and stagnation conditions.
If the back pressure is below $0.528\,p_0$ (air), a converging nozzle is choked and $M=1$ at the throat.
Use $\dot m_{max}=0.0404A^*p_0/\sqrt{T_0}$ for air with SI units.
Use $dA/A=(M^2-1)\,dV/V$ to decide whether a duct accelerates or decelerates the flow.

blocks.title: Choked flow depends only on upstream stagnation conditions
blocks.text: Once the throat is sonic, the mass flow rate depends only on $p_0$, $T_0$ and the throat area; it is proportional to $p_0$ and inversely proportional to $\sqrt{T_0}$. This is how flow meters and relief valves are sized.

blocks.title: Use absolute pressures and kelvin
blocks.text: Stagnation relations need absolute pressure (not gauge) and absolute temperature in kelvin. Also note that $T_0$ stays the same along an adiabatic flow, but the static temperature drops as the gas accelerates.

points: For a perfect gas, $T_0/T=1+\tfrac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2$ and $p_0/p=(T_0/T)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}$ in isentropic flow.
A converging nozzle chokes when the throat reaches $M=1$ (for air at $p_b/p_0\le0.528$), and the mass flow is then $\dot m_{max}\approx0.0404A^*p_0/\sqrt{T_0}$.
Subsonic flow accelerates in a converging duct; supersonic flow accelerates in a diverging duct, as $dA/A=(M^2-1)dV/V$.
The throat of a converging-diverging nozzle is the only place where $M=1$ can be reached smoothly.

questions.stem: What is the stagnation temperature of a gas stream?

options.text: The temperature of the walls of the duct
The temperature measured by a thermometer moving with the flow
The temperature the gas would have if brought to rest adiabatically
The temperature at which the gas reaches Mach 1

questions.correctOptionText: The temperature the gas would have if brought to rest adiabatically

distractorRationale.a: Wall temperature is a boundary condition and not related to total temperature.
distractorRationale.b: This is the static temperature, which is lower than T0 when the gas is moving.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it includes the kinetic energy converted to enthalpy, T0 = T + V^2/(2 cp).
distractorRationale.d: That is the sonic (critical) temperature T*, which is a different quantity.

questions.explanation: From the steady-flow energy equation for an adiabatic process $c_pT_0=c_pT+V^2/2$, so $T_0$ is the temperature after the kinetic energy has been fully converted into enthalpy by decelerating the flow to rest. A thermometer moving with the stream reads the lower static temperature.

questions.stem: Air (perfect gas, gamma = 1.4) flows at Mach 1.5 with a static temperature of 250 K. Find the stagnation temperature in kelvin.
Air (gamma = 1.4) flows at Mach 0.60 in a duct where the static pressure is 80.0 kPa. Assuming isentropic deceleration to rest, find the stagnation pressure in kPa.

A converging nozzle with a throat area of 3.0 cm^2 is supplied from a reservoir at 800 kPa (absolute) and 350 K and discharges into atmosphere at 101 kPa. Use gamma = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg K). The flow is choked. Find the mass flow rate in kg/s.
questions.explanation: Since 101/800 = 0.126 is below 0.528 the nozzle is choked. mdot = 0.0404 A* p0/sqrt(T0) = 0.0404 x 3.0e-4 x 8.0e5/sqrt(350) = 0.5185 kg/s (the exact expression gives 0.5185).

questions.stem: Air flows subsonically through a converging duct. What happens to its speed and static pressure as it moves through the duct?

options.text: Speed decreases and static pressure rises
Speed increases and static pressure falls
Speed decreases and static pressure falls
Speed increases and static pressure rises

questions.correctOptionText: Speed increases and static pressure falls

distractorRationale.a: This describes a subsonic diffuser (diverging duct).
distractorRationale.b: Correct: for M < 1, dA < 0 gives dV > 0, and dp = -rho V dV < 0.
distractorRationale.c: Pressure and speed are linked by dp = -rho V dV; they move in opposite directions.
distractorRationale.d: Rising pressure with rising speed would violate the momentum (Euler) relation.

questions.explanation: For $M<1$ the factor $(M^2-1)$ is negative, so $dA<0$ gives $dV>0$. The momentum relation $dp=-\rho V\,dV$ then gives falling static pressure.

questions.stem: Supersonic air (M > 1) enters a diverging duct with isentropic flow. What happens to its velocity and Mach number?

options.text: Both increase as the area grows
Velocity stays constant and only the pressure changes
Velocity increases but Mach number decreases
Both decrease as the area grows

questions.correctOptionText: Both increase as the area grows

distractorRationale.a: Correct: for M > 1, (M^2-1) is positive so dA > 0 gives dV > 0; Mach number also rises.
distractorRationale.b: Pressure change requires a velocity change through dp = -rho V dV.
distractorRationale.c: Mach number is V/a and a falls as T falls, so M rises even faster than V.
distractorRationale.d: This is the subsonic behaviour in a diverging duct.

questions.explanation: With $M>1$, $dA/A=(M^2-1)dV/V$ is positive for positive $dV$, so an expanding area accelerates the flow. As it speeds up, the temperature and speed of sound fall, so the Mach number increases even faster than the velocity.

questions.stem: Once a converging nozzle is choked, lowering the back pressure further does not increase the mass flow rate, provided the reservoir conditions and throat area stay fixed.
questions.explanation: At the choked condition the throat is sonic, so downstream pressure disturbances cannot travel upstream against the flow. The mass flow is then set by the upstream stagnation conditions and the throat area alone.

questions.stem: A choked nozzle passes mass flow m_dot. The reservoir temperature is quadrupled at the same stagnation pressure and throat area. What is the new choked mass flow rate?

distractorRationale.a: This confuses T0 with p0: m_dot is proportional to p0, not T0.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: m_dot is proportional to 1/sqrt(T0), so quadrupling T0 halves it.
distractorRationale.c: This would be the result if m_dot were proportional to 1/T0, which it is not.
distractorRationale.d: The mass flow falls with temperature because hot gas is less dense; it does not rise.

questions.explanation: The choked mass flow is $\dot m\propto A^*p_0/\sqrt{T_0}$. If $T_0$ is multiplied by 4, $\sqrt{T_0}$ doubles and the mass flow halves.

questions.stem: Derive the area-velocity relation dA/A = (M^2 - 1) dV/V for steady one-dimensional isentropic flow, and use it to explain why a converging-diverging nozzle is needed to accelerate a gas from subsonic to supersonic speed.
markingGuide: Continuity: rho V A = constant, so d rho/rho + dV/V + dA/A = 0
Isentropic speed of sound: dp = a^2 d rho, hence d rho/rho = - M^2 dV/V
Subsonic flow needs dA < 0 to accelerate; supersonic flow needs dA > 0 to accelerate
At M = 1, dA = 0, so sonic flow can only occur at the minimum-area throat: converge to reach M = 1 at the throat, then diverge to continue accelerating
questions.explanation: Combining continuity, the Euler equation and $dp=a^2d\rho$ gives $d\rho/\rho=-M^2dV/V$ and hence $dA/A=(M^2-1)dV/V$. Since the sign of $(M^2-1)$ changes at $M=1$, a duct that must accelerate subsonic gas through sonic speed to supersonic speed must first converge and then diverge.

questions.stem: A supersonic wind-tunnel test section has air at Mach 2.2 with static temperature 220 K and static pressure 120 kPa (absolute). Take gamma = 1.4 and R = 287 J/(kg K). (a) Calculate the flow speed. (b) Calculate the stagnation temperature and pressure that the reservoir must supply. (c) Explain why the stagnation temperature is much higher than the static temperature even though no heat is added.
markingGuide: Stagnation temperature includes the kinetic energy V^2/(2 cp) converted to enthalpy when the flow is brought to rest
No heat is needed: adiabatic deceleration converts kinetic energy into internal energy, raising the temperature
questions.explanation: The speed of sound at 220 K is 297.3 m/s, so V = 654 m/s. The stagnation temperature is 433.0 K and the stagnation pressure is 1283 kPa, because decelerating the gas to rest converts its kinetic energy $V^2/2$ (about 214 kJ/kg) into enthalpy.
